  Nato on Tuesday condemned “irresponsible nuclear rhetoric” by Russia, after Moscow warned it would “deploy its entire arsenal” if the alliance threatens its exclave Kaliningrad. “I can confirm that Russia sent a non-paper to Nato and that we have sent a response, noting that Nato is a defensive Alliance and none of our activities or exercises pose a risk to any part of Russia,” Allison Hart, a Nato spokesperson, said. “We strongly denounce the threat of force, including any irresponsible nuclear rhetoric. We call on Russia to end its unprovoked war in Ukraine.”
- 
  Russia has intensified daytime strikes on Kyiv using jet-powered drones that Ukrainian forces are struggling to intercept. Russia fired ballistic missiles and dozens of jet-powered drones at Kyiv, Ukraine’s air force said Tuesday, as Moscow seeks to make Ukraine buckle under the pressure of day-and-night bombardment of its capital and other cities. Russia has used new jet-powered drones that fly too fast and too high for Ukrainian ground-based air defenses to shoot down.
- 
  Russia struck two datacentres in Kyiv overnight, a military-linked cargo vessel in the Black Sea, and another vessel with military cargo in the Ukrainian port of Odesa, the Russian defence ministry said on Tuesday. In a later evening statement, the ministry said its forces had launched a drone strike on a ship in the Black Sea which it said was carrying cargo intended for the Ukrainian armed forces.
- 
  Ukraine’s top university on Tuesday said it was ordering students to stay home as it switched to remote classes due to the surge in Russian daytime drone attacks on the capital. Kyiv’s Taras Shevchenko National University said it would “switch to a remote format of work” until at least 16 October, “due to the deteriorating security situation in Kyiv”. The university’s main campus is close to the National Academy of Sciences, which was hit by a drone strike, killing one person, on Monday.
- 
  Russian glide bombs struck a school in the northern Ukrainian city of Sumy on Tuesday, killing two people and injuring six, the regional governor said. The city’s governor, Oleh Hryhorov, said three children were among the injured. He said teachers and school officials had managed to evacuate 100 people.
- 
  Russia’s foreign investment envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, met US officials in Washington for talks about future US-Russia energy projects planned after Moscow’s war against Ukraine, a US government official told AFP. Dmitriev and US officials held “constructive discussions on a peaceful resolution to the Russia-Ukraine conflict and possible US-Russia energy initiatives after the war ends” on Monday, the official said on Tuesday. “The visit follows special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner’s recent meeting with president Putin in Moscow and their discussions last week with Ukrainian officials in NYC,” said the official, speaking anonymously.
- 
  The US president, Donald Trump, favours a proposal under which the US would lift some sanctions if Russia released a number of political prisoners, according to a report in the Atlantic. The White House did not comment directly on the report. When asked about the article, a US official told AFP that Trump was “committed to continuing to play a constructive role in ending the war between Russia and Ukraine, and he remains optimistic that we’ll ultimately get a peace deal done”.
- 
  Russia will cut funding for welfare, education and healthcare in next year’s state budget to help cover soaring military spending, fiscal documents obtained by Reuters showed. Russia plans to spend 17.1tn roubles (US$202.58bn) on defence in 2027, about 27% more than the 13.5tn roubles originally budgeted and the highest figure since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022. Funding for social policy, which covers items such as state pensions, payments to war veterans and maternity benefits, will shrink by 7%, while education funding will fall by 6% and healthcare by 6.8%.
- 
  Belgium will transfer three F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine by the end of the year to help in its war with Russia, Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said on Tuesday. Zelenskyy said Ukraine had already received “urgent deliveries” of F-16 ammunition from Belgium and Spain, among other countries. Zelenskyy later said later Ukraine had received a “very good” assistance package the day before of a NASAMS air defence system, developed jointly in the US and Norway.
- 
  A Russian nuclear-capable strategic bomber crashed Tuesday on a training mission in the country’s far east, killing six members of its crew, its defence ministry said. The ministry said in a statement that the Tu-95 bomber went down in an unpopulated area in the Amur region, adding that one crew member survived the crash and was hospitalised with injuries.

NATO's Supreme Allied Commander Europe (SACEUR) Gen. Alexus Grynkewich 
NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe Gen. Alexus Grynkewich said Monday that any defense framework developed by the European Union should work alongside NATO rather than establish a competing system. Speaking at the European Parliament, he warned that parallel structures could increase costs and place further strain on limited defense resources.
Grynkewich said he had discussed proposals for a European defense union with several European leaders, stressing that the EU’s approach to defense organization should remain compatible with NATO’s existing command structure and military capabilities.
He argued that creating two separate systems would duplicate resources and expertise already available through NATO. “Whatever it is that the EU does with its member states and how it structures, should not be in competition with NATO,” he said.
Defense industry and procurement in focus
The NATO commander also highlighted the need for stronger coordination between the EU and NATO on defense production and procurement. He said decisions over where military equipment is manufactured have particular implications for companies from the US, Canada, UK, Norway and Türkiye.
Grynkewich cautioned against procurement policies that prioritize the country of origin of weapons and equipment over their military effectiveness. “A focus on where something is made rather than how well it performs in combat, how it performs on the battlefield, only benefits our adversaries,” he said.
Ankara forum showcases major agreements
Grynkewich pointed to a NATO defense industry forum held in Ankara, where hundreds of companies announced agreements with a combined value exceeding €50 billion, or nearly $57 billion.
The deals included projects involving strategic airlift and high-altitude intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance capabilities, according to the NATO commander. The Ankara gathering highlighted the scale of defense-industry cooperation within the alliance.
NATO and EU urged to combine capabilities
Grynkewich said closer NATO-EU coordination could allow both organizations to make better use of their respective strengths. He noted that the EU can provide financial and regulatory mechanisms, while NATO defines military requirements and brings established defense expertise.
“NATO and the EU are exponentially stronger when working together,” he said, calling for approaches that expand cooperation rather than create additional barriers between the two institutions.

articles.title: Board of Peace unveils Gaza recovery plan, Israel reports 18 ceasefire violations Sept. 15–29 - The Long War Journal
articles.summary: Board of Peace unveils Gaza recovery plan, Israel reports 18 ceasefire violations Sept. 15–29  The Long War Journal
articles.full_text:
On September 23, the US-backed Board of Peace (BoP) unveiled a $2.45 billion, six-month Gaza recovery plan, but its implementation remains stalled by disagreements over Hamas’s disarmament and Israel’s withdrawal. The following day, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu addressed the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA). Meanwhile, Israeli forces conducted numerous strikes over the past two weeks against Hamas commanders and financial operatives involved in the group’s efforts to reconstitute itself in Gaza.
The BoP announced its recovery plan for Gaza during a meeting on the sidelines of the UNGA in New York. The proposal includes 66 projects covering infrastructure, housing, healthcare, economic recovery, and security. Representatives from 35 countries and international organizations attended the meeting, where BoP executive board member Jared Kushner, US Special Envoy to the Middle East Steve Witkoff, BoP High Representative Nickolay Mladenov, and National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG) chief Ali Shaath discussed the transition from planning to implementation.
Shaath outlined a reconstruction strategy beginning in Rafah and expanding to Khan Younis, central Gaza, Gaza City, and northern Gaza as security conditions permit. However, the plan remains dependent on Hamas’s disarmament, the transfer of governing authority to the NCAG, and a phased Israeli withdrawal. The order of these phases represents the key sticking point in implementation.
Board officials acknowledged that negotiations with Israel remain difficult ahead of the October 27 Israeli election. Mladenov said that political considerations had made discussions more sensitive, although negotiations were making gradual progress. Witkoff insisted that there was no alternative to implementing the existing plan. The central unresolved dispute concerns the sequencing of Hamas’s disarmament and Israel’s withdrawal: Netanyahu insists that Hamas surrender its weapons before Israeli forces withdraw, while the proposed framework links disarmament to a phased withdrawal.
In a separate development, the BoP reaffirmed on September 25 that the United Nations Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA) would have no role in its Gaza reconstruction framework, arguing that the agency did not meet its requirements for trusted partners following reports of Hamas infiltration.
On September 24, Prime Minister Netanyahu addressed the UN General Assembly, defending Israel’s military campaigns against Hamas, Hezbollah, and Iran and rejecting international criticism of the war in Gaza. He credited US-Israeli military operations with severely damaging Iran’s nuclear facilities and military capabilities, predicted the eventual downfall of Iran’s government, and expressed support for Iranian protesters. Netanyahu also categorically rejected allegations that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza, arguing that Israeli forces have taken extensive measures to protect civilians while Hamas used them as human shields.
Netanyahu also criticized Qatar, Turkey and Western governments for their positions toward Israel, while rejecting Palestinian statehood under present circumstances. Dozens of delegates walked out as he began speaking, prompting him to call them “moral cowards.”
Meanwhile, in Gaza, Israel reported 18 operations against and ceasefire violations by Hamas and other Palestinian terror groups between September 15 and 29:
- On September 15, the IDF and Shin Bet announced that they killed Naal Abu Obaid, the commander of Hamas’s Rafah Brigade and head of operations in its military wing, in southern Gaza. Obaid succeeded Muhammad Shabana following his elimination and had previously served as the brigade’s deputy commander and commander of its Tel Sultan and Yebna battalions.
- On September 16, the IDF reported that it killed Jihad Smaeh Mahmoud Ismail, the commander of a Hamas Nukhba squad, in Khan Younis the previous week. Ismail had infiltrated Israel during the October 7 massacre and participated in the attack on an Israeli tank and the abduction of three Israeli soldiers, according to the Israeli military.
- Later the same day, the IDF announced that it killed Saeed Asaad Saeed Akram, a commander in Hamas’s Daraj Tuffah battalion, in northern Gaza. Akram had recently planted explosives and planned attacks against Israeli forces, according to the Israeli military. The IDF also reported killing two additional Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad (PIJ) operatives involved in attacks against its forces.
- On September 17, the IDF reported that it killed Shariff Shadi Ibrahim Labed, a Hamas Nukhba operative who participated in the October 7 assault on the Erez Crossing, in northern Gaza two days earlier. The military also announced the elimination of Yosef Saad al Din Rashid Zaim, a Hamas Nukhba commander, in a separate strike in northern Gaza earlier that week.
- Later the same day, the IDF announced that it killed Muhammad Jamal Ahmad Eid, a Hamas Nukhba commander who infiltrated Israel during the October 7 massacre, in Al Bureij the previous day. In a separate strike in Gaza City, the IDF killed Saleh Ziyad Ibrahim al Maqdad, a platoon commander in Hamas’s naval force, according to the Israeli military.
- On September 19, the IDF reported that it killed Muhammad Sulaiman Biuk, a Hamas commander who infiltrated Israel during the October 7 massacre, in Khan Younis two days earlier. Biuk had recently planted explosives, planned attacks against Israeli forces and civilians, and worked to rebuild Hamas’s military capabilities while violating the ceasefire, according to the Israeli military.
- On September 21, the IDF announced that an Israeli engineering vehicle struck an explosive device during routine operations near the Yellow Line, which separates the Israeli-controlled area of Gaza from the rest of the territory. No Israeli personnel were injured. The military described the incident as a violation of the ceasefire agreement and struck Hamas infrastructure in Gaza in response.
- On September 24, the IDF and Shin Bet announced that they killed Muhammad Abu Alwan, the head of Hamas’s finance department, in Khan Younis the previous day. Alwan had overseen the transfer of more than 1 billion shekels to Hamas during the war, financing its military operations and helping preserve its governing apparatus, according to the Israeli military.
- Later the same day, the IDF reported that it killed Mahmoud Abd al Fattah Awwad, a commander in Hamas’s military wing, in Gaza City the previous weekend. Awwad had participated in holding seven Israeli hostages, including Daniela Gilboa, Karina Ariev, and Doron Steinbrecher, in an underground tunnel during the war, according to the Israeli military.
- On September 25, the IDF announced that it killed Jaber Muqbil, a Hamas operative who led the Muqbil currency-exchange network, in Deir al Balah the previous day. The network had transferred millions of shekels in foreign currency to Hamas to finance its operatives and rebuild military infrastructure, according to the Israeli military. In a separate strike in Khan Younis, the IDF killed Hassan al Bata, a sniper in Hamas’s military wing.
- Later the same day, the IDF reported that it killed Hassan Mahmoud Siyam, a Hamas commander who infiltrated Israel during the October 7 massacre and subsequently participated in holding four Israeli hostages, including Amit Soussana and Keith Siegel, in captivity. The military also announced that it killed Adham Subhi Salem Ziyara, another Hamas operative, in a separate strike in Gaza City. Both had recently planned attacks against Israeli forces and participated in planting explosives near the Yellow Line, according to the IDF.
- On September 26, the IDF announced that it killed Ibrahim Fuzi Ismail Muhsan, the commander of a Hamas Nukhba platoon, in Nuseirat the previous day. The military also reported killing Muhammad Kamel Suleiman Muhsan, another Hamas operative, in Khan Younis. Both had recently planned attacks against Israeli forces and civilians and worked to rebuild Hamas’s military capabilities while violating the ceasefire, according to the IDF.
- On September 27, the IDF and Shin Bet announced that they killed Saher Nadal Latfi Zakr, the operative who drove the motorcycle used to abduct Noa Argamani and Avinatan Or from the Nova music festival during the October 7 massacre, in Nuseirat the previous day. Zakr belonged to “global jihadist organizations operating in the Gaza Strip” and had supplied Hamas with weapons during the war, according to the Israeli military.
- Later the same day, the IDF released footage that it said showed an operative using a child to transfer combat equipment into a civilian home in central Gaza. The military accused terrorist organizations in the territory of exploiting children to transport weapons and avoid Israeli strikes near the Yellow Line. The IDF said it refrained from striking the operative to prevent civilian casualties.
- Also on September 27, the IDF and Shin Bet reported that they killed Mohammed Hamed Mohammed Gubarin, a commander in Hamas’s military wing, in northern Gaza the previous week. Gubarin had participated in holding nine Israeli hostages, including Ziv Berman, Liri Albag, Agam Berger, and Alon Ohel, in captivity during the war, according to the Israeli military. He had recently planned attacks against Israeli forces and worked to rebuild Hamas’s military capabilities, the IDF said.
- On September 28, the IDF announced that it killed Adi Adli Abed al Atzar, a sniper in Hamas’s military wing, in southern Gaza the previous day. Atzar had recently planned attacks against Israeli forces and civilians and worked to rebuild Hamas’s military capabilities while violating the ceasefire, according to the Israeli military.

What is the Board of Peace? 
   What is Donald Trump’s plan for peace in the Gaza Strip? 
   What is the purpose of Israel’s ground offensive in Gaza City in September 2025? 
   Why did a United Nations report conclude that Israel has committed genocide in the Gaza Strip? 
   What was the immediate cause of the Israel-Hamas War? 
   How many people were killed during the October 7, 2023, attack? 
   What was the outcome of the brief ceasefire in January–March 2025? 
   What was the impact of the war on the Gaza Strip by November 2025? 
  News •
The Israel-Hamas War is a war in the Gaza Strip between Israel and Palestinian militants, especially Hamas, that began on October 7, 2023, when Hamas launched a land, sea, and air assault on Israel from the territory. The next day, Israel declared war for the first time since the Yom Kippur War (1973). Although Israel’s war objectives sought to dismantle Hamas and bring back the more than 240 people taken hostage during the October 7 attack, it later came under intense international criticism for the mounting death toll, which exceeded 70,000 in November 2025, and the widespread destruction throughout the Gaza Strip. Pressure on the Israeli government from abroad and at home, where many Israelis called for a ceasefire that would lead to an immediate return of the hostages, culminated eventually in a ceasefire agreement between Israel and Hamas in October 2025, which mediators hoped would bring an end to the war. The ceasefire went into effect on October 10, and the final surviving hostages were released on October 13.
The October 7, 2023, attack
The election of Hamas in 2006 and its subsequent takeover of the Gaza Strip in 2007 prompted Israel and Egypt to blockade the enclave. A series of short conflicts took place between Hamas and Israel, most notably in 2008, 2012, 2014, and 2021, but Israel generally considered the security threat from Hamas to be contained and manageable. With the conclusion in 2020 of the Abraham Accords, a set of normalization agreements between Israel and several Muslim-majority countries, the Arab states increasingly put aside the issue of Palestinian self-determination while other international actors, such as the United States, sought to shift global interest away from the Middle East to other regions. With the world’s eyes turned elsewhere, frustration was mounting in the Gaza Strip and the West Bank with the continued expansion of Israeli settlements, new provocations in Jerusalem around Al-Aqsa Mosque and in nearby neighborhoods, and, beginning in 2022, some of the worst confrontations between Israelis and Palestinians in the West Bank in decades. In late 2023 the United States was reportedly on the verge of concluding an agreement between Israel and Saudi Arabia to normalize relations, a development that was later considered to be a factor in the timing of the October 7 attack.
Hamas, along with other militants in the Gaza Strip, such as the Palestinian Islamic Jihad (PIJ), carried out the October 7 attack on Shemini Atzeret, a Jewish holiday that closes the autumn thanksgiving festival of Sukkot. Many soldiers of the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) were on leave, and its available forces were focused on protecting Israel’s northern border rather than on the Gaza Strip in the south, which analysts considered to be pacified.
The assault began about 6:30 am with a barrage of at least 2,200 rockets launched into Israel in just 20 minutes. During that opening salvo, Hamas used more than half the total number of rockets launched from Gaza during all of 2021’s 11-day conflict. The barrage reportedly overwhelmed the Iron Dome system, the highly successful antimissile defense system deployed throughout Israel, although the IDF did not specify how many missiles penetrated the system. As the rockets rained down on Israel, at least 1,500 militants from Hamas and the PIJ infiltrated Israel at dozens of points by using explosives and bulldozers to breach the border, which was heavily fortified with smart technology, fencing, and concrete. They disabled communication networks for several of the Israeli military posts nearby, allowing them to attack those installations and enter civilian neighborhoods undetected. Militants simultaneously breached the maritime border by motorboat near the coastal town of Zikim. Others crossed into Israel on motorized paragliders.
About 1,200 people were killed in the assault, which included families attacked in their homes in kibbutzim and attendees of an outdoor music festival. That number largely comprised Israeli civilians but also included foreign nationals. A March 2024 United Nations report found evidence that some were victims of sexual violence before they were killed. Adding to the trauma was the fact that it was the deadliest day for Jews since the Holocaust.
More than 240 people were taken into the Gaza Strip as hostages. Many of them were taken from their homes and some from the music festival. Including Israelis with dual citizenship, more than half of those taken hostage held passports from about two dozen countries.
The first year of war in the Gaza Strip (2023–24)
October 2023: Air campaign
At 8:23 am on October 7 the IDF announced a state of alert for war and began mobilizing its army reserves (eventually calling up more than 350,000 reservists over the next several days). Two hours later, IDF fighter jets began conducting air strikes in the Gaza Strip. On October 8 Israel declared itself in a state of war, and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told residents of the blockaded enclave to “get out now. We will be everywhere and with all our might.” On October 9 Israel ordered a “complete siege” of the Gaza Strip, cutting off water, electricity, food, and fuel from entering the territory. Following the recommendation of the Winograd Commission (2008), which investigated the missteps and failures of the 2006 Lebanon War, Netanyahu formed a war cabinet on October 11 comprised of him, defense minister Yoav Gallant, and opposition leader Benny Gantz.
As Israel conducted air strikes, international efforts were made to secure the release of the hostages. Qatar, which in years past had coordinated with Israel on the delivery of international aid packages to the Gaza Strip, became the key mediator, but in the first weeks of the war it managed to negotiate the release of only four of the people held by Hamas. Gaza’s subterranean tunnels—an intricate web of passageways extending hundreds of miles that had been built for smuggling and conducting raids—added to the difficulty of locating the hostages as well as targeting militants and their weapons caches: Destroying the tunnels without high civilian cost proved difficult, and conducting military activity inside the tunnels presented a high risk for all those inside, including the IDF troops and the hostages who might be held there. Just three weeks after Hamas’s assault on October 7, more than 1.4 million Palestinians in the Gaza Strip had become internally displaced, and it had also become the deadliest conflict for the Palestinians since the 1948 Arab-Israeli War.
October 2023–January 2024: Ground invasion and initial ceasefire efforts
The war entered a new chapter at the end of October when Israeli ground forces advanced into the Gaza Strip. Communications in the territory were initially cut, restricting the ability of militants to coordinate but also limiting the ability of paramedics and humanitarian organizations to attend to emergencies. Unlike in previous conflicts in the Gaza Strip, the ground invasion began slowly and the number of armored vehicles and personnel was increased gradually. On November 1 the Rafah border crossing between the Gaza Strip and Egypt was opened, under conditions agreed to by Egypt, Hamas, and Israel, to allow a limited number of foreign nationals to evacuate the territory for the first time since October 7.
The first agreement to pause fighting occurred just six weeks into the war, when on November 22 Israel and Hamas agreed to a prisoner exchange mediated by Qatar and Egypt. During the pause, which lasted seven days, 110 of the hostages were freed in exchange for 240 Palestinian prisoners. In the days after fighting resumed, Israeli forces moved into the city of Khan Younis. A large number of civilians fled to Rafah, the last major urban center in the enclave for civilians to shelter from the ground invasion, and within weeks more than half of the Gaza Strip’s total population had crammed into the city along Egypt’s border.
By year’s end international support for Israel’s response to the October 7 attack began to wane amid the high number of civilian casualties and wide destruction in the Gaza Strip. In early January 2024, after nearly 23,000 Palestinians had been reported dead (a number that included mostly civilians but also Hamas fighters), Israel announced a change in strategy that resulted in a steep reduction in the average number of daily deaths to about one-third of what it had been in October. But the number was still more than three times that of the 2014 conflict, the deadliest in the Gaza Strip until 2023.
In late January Qatar, Egypt, and the United States proposed a framework for a ceasefire that would be conducted in three phases, which laid the groundwork for future agreements. The pause would include the release, in stages, of hostages held in the Gaza Strip and Palestinian prisoners taken by Israel since the start of the conflict. But the framework did not include guarantees that the hostage exchange would lead to a permanent ceasefire, a condition Hamas continued to insist on in future proposals.
February–June 2024: Invasion of Rafah looms
The concerns over the war’s high human cost reached a new level in February 2024 when Israeli officials announced their intent to extend the war into Rafah, the only remaining refuge for civilians. Despite the international outcry—which included an unusual rift between Isr

articles.title: Israel-Hamas War - Ceasefire and hostage exchange (January–March 2025) - Britannica
articles.summary: Israel-Hamas War - Ceasefire and hostage exchange (January–March 2025)  Britannica
articles.full_text:
An agreement for a ceasefire and exchange of hostages was announced on January 15, 2025. The details of the ceasefire deal followed a three-phase approach. The first phase of the deal, lasting six weeks, included:
News •
- Cessation of hostilities
- Phased release of about 1,900 Palestinian prisoners
- Return of displaced Gazans to their homes beginning on the seventh day
- Increase in humanitarian aid to the Gaza Strip to 600 trucks per day
A second phase, whose details required additional negotiation during the first phase, would see the release of the remainder of living hostages held by Hamas, the release of additional Palestinian prisoners, a wider withdrawal of Israeli troops from the Gaza Strip, and the declaration of a permanent end to the war. The third phase would include the exchange of bodies of deceased hostages and fighters, the reconstruction of the Gaza Strip, and the opening of the Gaza Strip’s border crossings.
Despite the pause in fighting in the Gaza Strip, violence was ramped up in the West Bank, in part as a conciliatory measure made by Netanyahu for his far-right coalition partner Bezalel Smotrich to tolerate the ceasefire agreement. Smotrich also insisted Netanyahu promise that fighting in the Gaza Strip would eventually resume. Concerns about the fate of Palestinian civilians were heightened further when Trump in late January indicated he wanted to “just clean out” the Gaza Strip and relocate its residents abroad. Days later he said that the United States would own and build on the Gaza Strip and that Gazans would not return to the territory, because “they’ll be resettled in areas where they can live a beautiful life.” But where Gazans would be welcome and secure remained entirely unclear: Egypt and Jordan had already rejected requests from Trump to take in displaced Palestinians, and Saudi Arabia condemned a suggestion by Netanyahu that Gazans be relocated to Saudi Arabia. Following Trump’s comments, UN Secretary-General António Guterres reaffirmed the UN’s commitment to a two-state solution and warned against “any form of ethnic cleansing” and the “chilling, systematic dehumanization and demonization of an entire people.”
Implementation of the first phase
On January 19, after days of anticipation and uncertainty over the deal’s implementation, the first hostage release of the agreement took place as three Israeli women, two who had been kidnapped from their homes and the other from the music festival, were handed over to the International Committee of the Red Cross. Hours later 90 Palestinian prisoners—69 women and 21 teenage boys who had been convicted of minor offenses or held without charge—were released in Ramallah in the West Bank, completing the first exchange of the agreement.
The weekly exchanges continued to take place in the subsequent weeks. But tension brewed from the start as Hamas made a spectacle of the releases, parading the hostages who were set to be freed (some of whom smiled and waved to the crowds gathered to witness) and presenting them with signed documents authenticating their release. The events were choreographed in a way that exaggerated Hamas’s control over the Gaza Strip and distorted its treatment of the hostages as humane and dignified, and in propaganda it compared its treatment against that of Palestinian prisoners, some of whom appeared frail and emaciated upon release. That façade quickly crumbled in early February when three male hostages, who appeared pale and gaunt, were released.
Hamas also attempted to postpone its release of hostages, saying on February 10 that Israel was not allowing as much humanitarian aid into the Gaza Strip as it had promised. In response Netanyahu, with Trump’s encouragement, threatened to end the ceasefire if any of the remaining hostages were not released by February 15. Hamas later announced it would continue the hostage exchange as planned after mediators pledged to remove obstacles to the delivery of humanitarian aid. By the close of the first phase, 33 Israeli hostages and nearly 2,000 Palestinian prisoners had been released, as well as 5 Thai hostages held by Hamas who were not part of the formal agreement.
Breaking of the ceasefire
Although the original ceasefire agreement called for negotiations over the second phase to begin by the 16th day of the first phase (February 3), negotiations had still not taken place by the time the first phase ended on March 2. An informal truce remained in place through mid-March, even as Israel, which demanded the immediate release of hostages who were set to be returned under the ceasefire’s second phase, renewed its blockade of humanitarian aid and cut off electricity to the territory. Netanyahu, facing pressure within his coalition to resume the war, sought to avoid a confrontation with his political allies ahead of a looming deadline for a national budget at the end of March. With backing from the United States, he allowed the fighting to resume.
Return to hostilities (March–October 2025)
Israel renewed its campaign on March 18 with a fresh bombardment of the Gaza Strip, killing more than 400 people. The next day it launched an operation to bisect the Gaza Strip by retaking the Netzarim Corridor, a line of Israeli military assets just south of Gaza City that Israeli forces had removed as part of the ceasefire agreement. The creation weeks later of a new military corridor between Khan Younis and Rafah, called the Morag Corridor, further divided the Gaza Strip and isolated Rafah. Israeli forces ordered the evacuation of nearly all of Rafah in April in what it said was an operation to clear the city of Hamas combatants and infrastructure. In early May Netanyahu’s war cabinet announced a plan, set to begin in late May, to vastly expand Israeli operations and move the entirety of the population southward toward Rafah. The plan controversially included the distribution of aid at a limited number of sites in southern Gaza by the newly created Gaza Humanitarian Foundation (GHF), a private organization set up to centralize aid-distribution efforts under the supervision of the United States and Israel. By that time the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) projected that more than half of the Gaza Strip’s population was facing emergency food insecurity and one-fifth of the population was already facing catastrophe or famine.
The Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) scale is used to classify food insecurity by many of the most prominent international humanitarian aid organizations, including the World Food Programme (WFP), the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), and the World Health Organization (WHO). Here’s a summary of what each phase means:
- Phase 1 (None/Minimal): Ability to meet essential food and nonfood needs.
- Phase 2 (Stressed): Ability to meet minimally adequate food needs but unable to afford some essential nonfood needs.
- Phase 5 (Catastrophe/Famine): Extreme lack of food or other basic needs after exhausting all emergency strategies, marked by starvation, death, destitution, and extreme acute malnutrition.
Meanwhile, the United States began engaging in direct talks with Hamas, particularly over the release of the last remaining hostage with American citizenship, Edan Alexander. The move, which was the first time direct talks between the United States and the U.S.-designated terrorist group had taken place in an official capacity, prompted concerns from Israeli officials that the Trump administration was not fully committed to backing Israel in the conflict. That the United States was pursuing its own priorities in the Middle East became apparent when it announced a ceasefire with the Houthi movement on May 6, just two days after a Houthi missile struck the international airport near Tel Aviv. Israeli officials were reportedly blindsided by the announcement of the deal, which did not require Houthi forces to end hostilities with Israel. On May 12, the eve of Trump’s first trip to the Middle East in his second presidential term, Hamas released Alexander as a gesture that Trump hailed on Truth Social as a “step taken in good faith” toward ending the war. Notably absent from Trump’s itinerary was a visit with any Israeli officials.
At the end of May headway was made toward a more lasting ceasefire. Witkoff proposed a plan that required negotiations for a permanent ceasefire to begin on the first day and gave Trump a special role in enforcing the ceasefire. Israeli officials agreed to the plan, but Hamas leaders rejected it, saying they did not consider its guarantees toward a permanent truce sufficiently credible and that its protocols for humanitarian aid were inadequate. Still, the plan was very close in form and detail to the ceasefire arrangement agreed to in October later that year.
A 12-day conflict in June led to the most dramatic transformation of the regional landscape since the conflict with Hezbollah in the previous year. Israel bombarded Iran’s military infrastructure and, with assistance from the United States, severely damaged its nuclear program. The attacks not only caused significant damage to Iran’s nuclear program, which was one of Israel’s foremost security concerns, but also diminished its air defense and missile capabilities, which in turn hurt its ability to aid allies like Hamas. Netanyahu characterized the development as opening “many opportunities” for Israel, including in the resumption of negotiations for the release of hostages in the Gaza Strip. Talks remained at an impasse, however, and in late July the United States and Israel withdrew their delegations from the negotiations.
Meanwhile, international pressure mounted on Israel to loosen its restrictions on humanitarian aid. By late July more than 1,000 Gazans had been killed by gunfire while trying to get food from GHF sites or other sources of aid distribution, according to the United Nations. articles.title: Over 77 Percent of Ransomware Groups are targeting the Healthcare Sector - Cybersecurity Insiders
articles.summary: Over 77 Percent of Ransomware Groups are targeting the Healthcare Sector  Cybersecurity Insiders
articles.full_text:
Ransomware attacks have emerged as one of the most persistent cybersecurity threats facing organizations across industries. While no sector appears to be completely immune to such attacks, the healthcare industry has increasingly become a prime target for ransomware groups.
According to a recent survey, more than 77 percent of ransomware groups are reportedly targeting organizations within the healthcare sector, highlighting the growing cybersecurity risks faced by hospitals, healthcare providers, insurers and other organizations that handle sensitive medical information.
According to the US Ransomware Industry Targeting Report released by Anomali, an AI-based threat intelligence platform, more than 200 ransomware variants and groups targeted organizations across eight major industries during the 2025–2026 period. Healthcare emerged as the most frequently targeted sector, followed by manufacturing and education.
The growing threat is particularly concerning because healthcare organizations possess enormous volumes of highly sensitive and valuable information. Unlike many other forms of data, medical records cannot simply be replaced once they are stolen or leaked.
Healthcare organizations routinely store patient information, clinical records, health insurance details, payment information, prescription data and employee records. This makes healthcare databases particularly attractive to cyber criminals looking to steal information, disrupt operations or demand ransom payments.
The situation has also become more complicated amid heightened geopolitical tensions during 2026. Since February, cyber threat activity has been closely watched against the backdrop of escalating tensions involving the United States and Iran, including concerns surrounding the security of fuel transportation through the Strait of Hormuz. Such geopolitical developments can create additional opportunities for cyber criminal groups and state-linked threat actors to exploit organizations and critical infrastructure.
The healthcare sector’s vulnerability, however, extends beyond the value of the information it stores. Many healthcare providers operate complex and highly interconnected IT environments that include legacy systems, specialized medical equipment and devices that may be difficult or impossible to patch without disrupting essential services. Replacing or upgrading such systems can also be expensive and operationally challenging.
At the same time, healthcare organizations are increasingly dependent on digital systems for everything from patient registration and electronic health records to laboratory services, medical imaging, billing and communication. A successful ransomware attack can therefore have consequences that extend far beyond data loss. It can disrupt routine operations, delay medical procedures, affect patient care and potentially force organizations to divert resources toward recovering their systems.
These characteristics make the healthcare industry an especially attractive target for ransomware operators. The combination of valuable data, interconnected systems, legacy technology and the need to maintain uninterrupted services can increase the pressure on organizations to restore access quickly.
The findings underline the need for healthcare organizations to strengthen their cybersecurity defenses, regularly assess vulnerabilities, maintain effective backup systems and develop robust incident-response plans. As ransomware groups continue to evolve their tactics, protecting healthcare infrastructure will require not only stronger technology but also continuous monitoring, employee awareness and coordinated efforts across the cybersecurity ecosystem.

articles.title: NATO uses fighter jets to stop drones. One ally says a Ukraine-inspired defense will handle them first. - Business Insider
articles.summary: NATO uses fighter jets to stop drones. One ally says a Ukraine-inspired defense will handle them first.  Business InsiderNATO’s front line now stretches across Europe, top commander warns  stripes.comSecretary General and Lithuanian Prime Minister discuss eastern flank defence, drones and support for Ukraine  North Atlantic Treaty Organization | NATOOptions for a NATO Multinational Drone-Interception Squadron  Royal United Services Institute (RUSI)NATO chi...
articles.full_text:
Fighter jets armed with expensive air-to-air missiles have led the way in the fight to take down the cheap drones that breach NATO airspace, a costly dynamic officials say needs to change.
NATO ally Latvia is building a Ukraine-inspired automated anti-drone wall along its entire eastern border with Russia. It is designed to make fighter jets a last line of defense, not the first, Latvian Defense Minister Raivis Melnis told Business Insider. The system is expected to be completed by the end of September.
The system, Melnis said, aims to detect and neutralize "any drone which flies in." Fighter jets will work instead as "the secondary means" of stopping drones, he said. If a drone penetrates the wall, NATO jets will then be used to intercept it.
Latvia's approach is aimed at addressing a problem facing NATO more broadly: relying on fighter jets such as F-35s, F-16s, and Rafales to shoot down cheap drones with air-to-air missiles can prove expensive. Surface-to-air missiles can be even more costly, putting defenders in an unsustainable situation.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said in June that "long-term we cannot continue by shooting down drones with very costly interceptors, so we have to find interception techniques which are of the same costs as the drones."
It's a problem the US has worried about in its war with Iran, where some Iranian drones were stopped by very expensive interceptor missiles.
Melnis said it's important that drones are stopped by a "cheap but reliable system." He described interceptor drones, which the Ukrainians have pioneered as a cost-effective defense, as "a cheap technology in comparison with a missile."
A border that stops drones
Melnis said that the new anti-drone border is key because ultimately, the "border is not a Russian-Latvian border. It is a Russia-NATO, Russia-Europe border."
He said that while this segment of Russia's border is shared specifically with Latvia, "we are NATO, and we are a European Union country." Any drone that crosses the border, he said, "that's the drone coming into NATO airspace. That's the drone coming into Europe."
The defensive plan was inspired by Ukraine, which has developed a host of cheap interceptor drones to stop Russian attack drones without using expensive air defense missiles. That development has been a wake-up call across Europe.
Latvia still values NATO's air-policing missions, which bring aircraft and pilots from across the alliance to defend its airspace. Those missions have expanded at Latvia's request in response to recent drone incursions.
But Russia's war against Ukraine has demonstrated the limitations of relying on expensive defenses against cheap drones, which can be launched in large numbers and overwhelm air defenses.
Melnis said that the goal is for soldiers to make only "the final decision to neutralize" a drone. "Otherwise, detection, tracking, and launching, that's autonomous," he said, allowing Latvia to rely on technology to reduce the number of soldiers needed to operate the system.
Learning from Ukraine's counter-drone warfare
NATO allies are turning to cheaper air defenses, such as interceptor drones, and learning lessons from Ukraine; however, most are still far from fielding new solutions at scale. Latvia is moving especially quickly.
Melnis said that Latvia's defense planning was driven by observations and lessons from the war in Ukraine, where interceptor drones are proving to have a "really high reliability and kill ratio" against the threat of Russian drones.
Latvia is keenly focused on preparing for Russian aggression. It has been facing what it calls hybrid attacks, including cyber attacks, arson, espionage, and disinformation campaigns. Moscow has also threatened military action against the country.
Melnis said Latvia is not seeing any Russian direct military aggression or conventional threat against Latvia or any other NATO member, but Russia is attempting to "break our cohesion, unity, break our will to support Ukraine."
He said supporting Ukraine, which Latvia has strongly backed, helps protect Latvia and the rest of NATO by keeping Russia from advancing and rebuilding its forces. Latvia is closely studying Ukraine's battlefield experience and working with Ukrainian defense companies to apply those lessons at home.
Latvia, he said, should "look at those lessons and then decide what's the best practice for us to take," rather than simply copying Ukraine. He said Ukraine can help NATO "build an understanding of how to fight such a war like they are fighting and to build our capabilities to be ready for a war," though a conflict involving Latvia, as a NATO ally, could look very different from Ukraine's war.

articles.title: Strategic Arms Limitation Talks | Cold War Arms Control Negotiations - Britannica
articles.summary: Strategic Arms Limitation Talks | Cold War Arms Control Negotiations  Britannica
articles.full_text:
The Strategic Arms Limitation Talks (SALT) were crucial U.S.-Soviet negotiations aimed at limiting nuclear weapons production. Beginning in 1969, SALT led to agreements like the 1972 ABM Treaty, restricting anti-ballistic missiles, and the Interim Agreement, freezing ICBM and SLBM levels. SALT II, signed in 1979, set limits on strategic launchers and MIRVs.
SALT I's ABM treaty limited each side to two ABM deployment areas, each with 100 interceptor missiles. These limitations prevented either party from defending more than a small fraction of its entire territory and thus kept both sides subject to the deterrent effect of the other’s strategic forces.
These talks were essential to détente, easing Cold War tensions, and fostering cooperation. Though SALT II faced setbacks, both sides still observed its arms limits. SALT helped stabilize mutual deterrence by permitting the Soviets to achieve parity.

articles.title: NATO says Russian hybrid campaign not stopping support for Ukraine - Euronews.com
articles.summary: NATO says Russian hybrid campaign not stopping support for Ukraine  Euronews.comEurope on edge from threats of Russia's growing escalation. Can NATO defend itself? : Sources & Methods  NPRTop NATO commander urges states to condemn Russian acts of sabotage  ReutersRussia could attack a NATO country within months, Danish intelligence warns  cnbc.comRussia’s escalating hybrid campaign against Europe  ft.com
articles.full_text:
European countries have already faced multiple incursions by Russian drones as well as a campaign of covert Russian disruption which began after Putin’s invasion of Ukraine.
NATO chief Mark Rutte urged "calm" on Tuesday over Russia's campaign of sabotage in Europe, saying it was failing to undercut support for Ukraine.
His comments come after Estonia became the latest country to officially blame Russia for such an incident, saying Moscow's "special services" had ordered an arson attack on a defence firm in August.
"Russia continues its reckless campaign of hostile actions against NATO allies. It is trying to weaken our resolve and stop our support for Ukraine. But Russia is failing. It is failing on the battlefield in Ukraine and it is failing to undermine our unity and support for Ukraine," Rutte told journalists.
European governments say Moscow is stepping up a campaign of sabotage and interference against Ukraine's backers as the Kremlin's troops struggle on the front line there, more than four years after their February 2022 invasion.
The Estonian incident came just after the discovery of an explosive-laden drone at an airport in Russia that Berlin pinned on Moscow.
Rutte admitted that Russia's activities "can have an impact and sometimes they have an impact, clearly."
But he urged NATO countries to remain "calm, carry on and support Ukraine."
"We should not be naive... about Russia, but they know we are stronger," Rutte said.
Speaking alongside the NATO chief, Lithuania's Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius said intelligence services had no proof Moscow was imminently prepping for something bigger.
"It's a must to say if a threat is there for society, but you can't exaggerate and say something is happening in the upcoming months or weeks," he said.
"The risk remains, but it's not fluctuating...not increasing or decreasing."
Earlier on Tuesday, Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna accused Russia of "sabotage" following an arson attack on the premises of defence company, Milrem Robotics, in August.
"We can conclude with certainty that the arson attack...in Tallinn was an act of sabotage ordered by the special services of the Russian Federation," he wrote in a post on X.
He added that the perpetrators of the attack had been apprehended and "no longer pose a threat" and that Estonia had summoned the Russian ambassador.
"This act of sabotage is part of Russia's broader campaign across Europe, aimed at intimidating us and weakening our support for Ukraine," Tsahkna wrote.
Estonia, an EU and NATO member state along the alliance's eastern flank, has accused Russia of several "hybrid" provocations since the beginning of Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Along with its neighbours, Latvia and Lithuania, it has ramped up its investment in defence in the years since and remains a staunch ally of Kyiv.
News of the attack prompted messages of solidarity from across Europe.
Germany’s Foreign Minister Johan Wadephul slammed what he called “Russia’s reckless act of hostility and said Estonia had full solidarity from Berlin.
French President Emmanuel Macron said in a post on X that "Russia must know that it will not prevail over either our unity or our determination to continue supporting Ukraine."
"The proliferation of these hostile acts reflects a dangerous escalation on the part of Russia, which will only lead it into a dead end," he added.
Sweden’s Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson called the attack “extremely serious.”
“This pattern of attacks is directed against Europe as a whole. The aim is to weaken our support for Ukraine and to intimidate us. It will not work,” he said in a post on X.
And the European Union said it stands by member state Estonia following the "reckless" arson attack and would not be put off supporting Ukraine.
"We stand by Estonia on this reckless attack," European Commission spokesperson Christian Wigand said, expressing "full solidarity" with Tallin.
"Moscow is trying to scare Europe into winding down its support for Ukraine. This will not happen," he added.
The Kremlin rejected what it called Estonia's "baseless" accusation that Russia ordered the arson attack in Tallinn.
"Such statements are baseless, ill-considered, have absolutely no relation to reality and lack any form of reasoning. Consequently, we cannot and will not take such statements seriously," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
Putin trying to break NATO support for Ukraine, leaders say
Putin, Stringer said, is “looking at a whole number of things” to try to create division between NATO allies because his campaign in Ukraine is going badly.
Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal likened the Russian leader to a “rat in the corner," who is escalating activity in Europe in an attempt to break Western support for Kyiv at a time when Moscow is under pressure.
Putin is trying to undermine NATO’s collective defence pact by testing nations with covert attacks that are hard to attribute, Michal said.
But the Estonian leader said it's currently “improbable,” that Putin will launch a conventional military attack on Europe because of the threat of a NATO response and because his forces are tied down in Ukraine.
The high level of malign activity from Russia is “here to stay” until Putin changes his military goals, Michal said, adding that the best way to deter him is to “back Ukraine.”

Google Earth has updated its images to show the devastating scale of destruction across Gaza with swathes of the strip reduced to rubble.
Israeli’s military action in Gaza has led to the damage and destruction of the majority of housing, hospitals, schools, and buildings across the 141 square mile territory, which is widely considered one of the most densely populated areas in the world.
Benjamin Netanyahu’s government has not allowed foreign journalists, independent investigators or several human rights groups into the strip. The Independent’s Bel Trew flew over the war-torn region last year and noted the “torched ruins of once-bustling cities” leaving Gaza in “ash and ruin”.
“It is as if giants have torn through anything that once lived here: monstrous teeth have ripped chunks out of the few buildings that still teeter above ground. Everything else appears stamped underfoot,” she said.
Barry Andrews, Member of the European Parliament for the Dublin constituency wrote: “The updated Google satellite images of Gaza are quite incredible, for all to see...” as social media users noticed that the images appeared to have been refreshed.
It was initially unclear when exactly the images had been updated but Google told The Independent that the most recent imagery was published in June 2026, adding: “We update satellite imagery from our third-party providers on a regular basis.”
Earlier this month, the UN called for international investigators to be granted access to all areas of Gaza to help collect evidence and document alleged violations as human remains continued to be uncovered from underneath the rubble.
Satellite images had previously documented the scale of the devastation but the new images show the most updated record of the damage inflicted across the region.
A United Nations report released last week concluded that Gaza is facing the worst economic crisis in history. It said that 90 per cent of working-age Palestinians are unemployed and that Annual GDP per capita had plummeted to $212 ($0.58 per day).
Only 1.5 per cent of arable land is now accessible for Palestinians with agricultural and industrial activity down by 94 per cent.
Earlier this year, the Red Cross told The Independent that there is only one fully functioning digger to help clear the rubble across the whole territory. Thousands are expected to be buried underneath.
Gaza’s forensic evidence team told The Independent earlier this year that a lack of DNA testing has left hundreds of bodies unidentified, with at least 1,129 recovered from underneath the rubble but left unnamed.
There is an estimated 60 million tonnes of debris spread across Gaza as a result of Israeli bombing across the territory.
Experts say that clearing the rubble could take decades but could be done in seven years if the correct resources were deployed.
The World Health Organisation estimates 90 per cent of hospitals have been damaged or destroyed. Around 82 per cent of all structures and more than 90 per cent of housing units have been damaged or destroyed, according to the United Nations Satellite Centre (UNOSAT).
Meanwhile, almost all of the population remains homeless with some surviving in the remains of collapsed buildings.
At least 21 people were killed earlier this month when a building caved in on Palestinian families sheltering there. Eight children were also killed in the collapse.
A CBC News investigation found satellite imagery appearing to show Israel compacting and removing rubble and debris from Gaza, that could contain human remains and potential evidence of war crimes across several sites.
A UN expert warned that Israel’s rubble-clearing could erase traces of the atrocity of crimes.
In an investigation earlier this year, the Geneva-based Euro-Med Monitor told The Independent that the remains of three brothers, killed in a suspected Israeli sniper attack as they crawled towards a hospital, had been cleared by Israeli bulldozers.
“The ongoing removal, crushing and relocation of rubble in Gaza must not destroy evidence of international crimes or prevent the recovery and identification of human remains in the besieged enclave,” said Francesca Albanese, special rapporteur on the situation of human rights in the Occupied Palestinian Territories.
“The implications are profound. Gaza’s rubble contains human remains and physical evidence relevant to the investigation of alleged international crimes, including genocide.”
Israel denies it is committing war crimes and has labelled accusations of genocide “antisemitic”.

articles.title: The New Forever War
articles.summary: Why America and Iran fight on without victory.
articles.full_text:
When will the war in Iran end? American officials claim that the answer is soon. “I think the war is going to end immediately after the [November] election,” declared U.S. President Donald Trump in September. “They can’t hold out any longer.” Iranian leaders agree that the war’s conclusion is near. Tehran has “brought the most heavily armed army in the history of the world to its knees,” proclaimed Ahmad Vahidi, the commander in chief of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, in August. Many outside analysts think that the conflict will drag on for longer and end with negotiations rather than with a clear winner. But generally, there is a sense that the fighting will soon be resolved, one way or another.
Such thinking is understandable. All wars eventually end, and after months of rising energy prices, the world is especially eager for this one to stop. Yet the unsettling reality is that the conflict is nowhere near over. The war’s two principal belligerents cannot achieve their desired goals, yet they both feel they are accomplishing enough to make continued fighting through a mix of military and economic tools worth it. The United States cannot topple the Iranian regime, get it to give up its missile program, force it to abandon its nuclear program, or make it stop supporting its regional partners. But Washington can keep degrading Iran’s military and constricting its economy. Iran cannot evict the world’s only superpower from the Middle East. Yet it can keep damaging U.S. regional bases, bombing the United States’ regional allies, and disrupting international commerce.
Critically, both states have the resources needed to fight indefinitely—and both believe they have no choice but to use them. They think that if their side lets up, the other will press on until it has either humiliated them or achieved its main objectives. They carry out periodic talks, but there is no mutual trust. In fact, they suspect that their enemy will simply use a cease-fire to regroup and resupply before attacking again. The Iranian government fears that relinquishing leverage, whether over Hormuz, its missile arsenal, or the nuclear program, would leave it exposed to pressure later. Washington, for its part, worries that sweeping sanctions relief would provide Tehran with the resources and time it needs to reconstitute its capabilities. Israel, meanwhile, fears that restraint today would only create a stronger Iran tomorrow. The steps required to escape the war look dangerous precisely because they require each side to temporarily make itself more vulnerable.
The war, then, will carry on as it has. There will not be a comprehensive resolution. There will be no lasting peace deal. But because the status quo is sustainable for each side, and because the parties lack the power to seize the upper hand, there will be no dramatic escalation, either. Tehran and Washington won’t be defeated. Yet no one will win.
NO WAY OUT
For the United States, the war was not supposed to go like this. When it joined Israel in striking the Islamic Republic on February 28, Washington thought that it would quickly prevail. The two countries, after all, had buried or destroyed most of Iran’s nuclear facilities and blown up many of its missile sites in June 2025. Israel had killed scores of senior Iranian scientists and more than two dozen military leaders, and it had decimated Hezbollah in Lebanon. Syrian President Bashar al-Assad—a longtime Iranian ally—had lost power, and massive protests had just rocked the Iranian government itself. The U.S. military and the Israel Defense Forces enjoyed what seemed like uncontested access to Iranian airspace. The regime, in other words, appeared to be on the precipice.
In the conflict’s opening days, Israel and the United States killed Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and many of the country’s top military commanders. But predictions that the Islamic Republic would collapse proved incorrect. The regime quickly replaced lost officials and set about striking back at its enemies, blowing up American jets, missile launchers, and radar systems on bases scattered throughout the Persian Gulf. It took control of the Strait of Hormuz and squeezed commercial flows through the waterway. And Iranian forces attacked civilian infrastructure across the Gulf region, making Washington’s regional partners pay for enabling the U.S.-Israeli assault.
American officials have downplayed these setbacks, promising that the Iranian regime is just one more strike or sanction away from being forced to make concessions. But it is extremely unlikely that Israel and Washington will force Tehran to compromise on anything significant. They have repeatedly tried to bomb the regime’s officials and military programs out of existence, only for Tehran to rapidly rebuild them. It is hard to see how future airstrikes can accomplish what past ones haven’t.
The United States, of course, has added a new dimension to its assault, piling on sanctions to accompany its blockade of Iran’s southern coast and periodic bombings. These measures have succeeded in further constricting Iran’s access to global markets, including its ability to import various wares and export key commodities such as oil. But this, too, is unlikely to persuade the regime. Overland routes and the Caspian Sea conspire against any attempt to hermetically seal Iran, even if the capacity of these passageways cannot compensate for the closing of naval routes and dwindling air links. China and Russia have provided a variety of goods and valuable military intelligence. The economic effect of the U.S. cutoffs is real, but the government will pass on the damage to its people by reducing subsidies rather than curbing spending on military and security services, which it needs to defend against external adversaries and internal dissent. The public must contend head-on with a collapsing currency and runaway inflation, and to ordinary Iranians, describing the present situation as sustainable would sound almost obscene. But what might be unsustainable for Iranian society can be perfectly sustainable for the state. The Islamic Republic does not need to protect Iran as a whole from economic deterioration. It must protect only the institutions and constituencies necessary for its own survival.
U.S. officials may hope that as Iran’s population becomes poorer, Tehran will have a change of heart. But Iranian leaders believe they are confronting an existential challenge, and in such circumstances, leaders are unlikely to regard any level of economic hardship as a clear breaking point. Plus, the regime has endured a worse situation without blinking, and for a longer time. From 1980 to 1988, the country fought a war with Iraq that killed hundreds of thousands of Iranians and left the state with hundreds of billions of dollars in damage. But even that was not enough to make Tehran quit. In fact, even after Iran expelled Iraqi forces from its territory, it invaded its adversary and spent six years trying to topple Iraqi President Saddam Hussein, despite continued domestic suffering. It took Iraqi battlefield advances, growing U.S. involvement in the Gulf, and a perception that the regional balance of power was moving sharply against Tehran to bring the conflict to a halt.
The United States, of course, has not played all its cards. It could put boots on the ground. But such operations would probably result in far more U.S. casualties and drive energy prices even higher. For these reasons, they are politically infeasible. Washington could launch airstrikes against major infrastructure targets, causing generational damage to Iran’s energy network, transportation and communications systems, and other facilities. But Tehran would retaliate in kind against American partners in the Gulf, also spiking energy costs.
Iran’s regime has celebrated its resilience in the face of U.S. attacks. But its prospects for defeating the United States look similarly grim. The country cannot easily increase the pressure because its economic distress narrows the margin for strategic recklessness. Iran’s leadership may believe it can survive prolonged hardship, yet another major confrontation with the United States would risk deeper damage amid an already strained social compact. Just as important, Iranian officials have little reason to believe that dramatic escalation would compel Washington to retreat; it could just as easily trigger a far more destructive response from an impulsive U.S. president. For now, Tehran is therefore likely to prefer imposing calibrated costs on the United States, preserving leverage, and testing American resolve without crossing a threshold that prompts intensive attacks.
And even if Tehran did dramatically escalate, the Islamic Republic is unlikely to triumph. Iran can weaken the United States’ regional footprint, and it has already forced the country to spend enormous sums—over $40 billion and counting—on the conflict. Yet the overall U.S. budget is in the trillions of dollars, and Washington has a large stockpile of less sophisticated bombs it could use to fight back as it runs low on advanced ones. It has lost troops, but only a tiny fraction of what it lost in Afghanistan and Iraq. And it can keep casualties relatively low because it can fight from a distance, lobbing missiles from outside Iranian territory.
STRAIT OF EQUILIBRIUM
At first, the fact that neither Tehran nor Washington can win outright might seem to bode well for peace. When countries realize that victory is unachievable, they sometimes settle. But both Iran and the United States have secondary aims, and they believe that continuing to fight will help achieve them. Washington, for example, thinks that occasional attacks will ensure that Tehran can never fully regenerate its military or develop nuclear weapons. It wants to strike Iran whenever the regime crosses a particular threshold, such as by rebuilding a particularly concerning weapons sys

articles.title: How Iran Changed War
articles.summary: The lessons of Tehran’s use of precise mass.
articles.full_text:
When the United States began bombing Iran, it expected to quickly overwhelm the country’s government. In the war’s first 24 hours, American and Israeli forces hit roughly 1,000 targets. Over the following 37 days, they blew up 12,000 more, laying waste to much of Iran’s military infrastructure. The strikes killed Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, Iran’s minister of defense, and the head of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
But more than six months later, the Iranian regime not only remains intact; it is perhaps stronger than before. It immediately replaced lost officials and struck back at Washington and its regional partners. And it shuttered the Strait of Hormuz, driving up energy prices around the world and winning newfound political leverage—all to the great frustration of U.S. officials.
There are several reasons why Iran performed surprisingly well. For one, the country had long planned for American and Israeli attacks, so it was prepared to reconstitute its government when top leaders were killed. It was also able to import enough goods to keep its economy from completely collapsing despite a U.S. naval blockade. But one of the most significant factors is that the Islamic Republic had built up a large arsenal of cheap yet accurate drones and missiles. These munitions made Iran’s counterattacks effective and allowed it to close the strait—and thus deter American escalation.
In doing so, Iran has demonstrated something broader. The age of what I called precise mass—or high-volume, low-cost, precision-guided weapons—is well underway. It is no longer possible for the U.S. military, or any military, to win a full-blown war simply by using small numbers of exquisite weapons to dazzle opponents. Weaker countries can match stronger ones through offensive barrages. Offense is currently cheaper than defense: the price of effective interceptors has yet to fall to the level of attack drones and missiles, which means defending against precise mass is extremely costly. After all, militaries cannot endlessly block salvos of $35,000 Shahed-136 attack drones with $4 million Patriot missiles.
To be sure, the war in Iran also shows that advanced technology remains essential. The United States, for example, had great success hitting valuable Iranian sites because it has artificial intelligence systems that can identify and recommend targets faster than ever before. American exquisite weapons are still much harder to stop than cheaper ones, and they are more likely to destroy targets in a single strike. But the world is learning from Iran, building on what Ukraine had already made clear: the future of war lies in part in precise mass. Everyone will now embrace the imperative of producing and using hosts of cheap and disposable weapons systems, changing warfare and the military balance.
SET IN ONE’S WAYS
In war, it might seem as if wealthy states always benefit from new military capabilities. But the reality is more complicated. If a new system is expensive, it indeed favors rich incumbents. But if it is cheap and demands large organizational changes to adopt, other countries can take advantage just as quickly—if not faster. In fact, the most powerful militaries in the world often struggle in the face of required disruptive organizational change, as their prior success has created bureaucracies and organizational biases that make adoption harder. As a result, they have a hard time integrating new capabilities that cannot be plugged into their existing structures.
Precise mass is just such a capability. The most conventionally powerful militaries are organized around small numbers of exquisite, expensive, hard-to-produce weapons and platforms such as Tomahawk missiles and F-35s. Their units train and plan around these systems. They thus cannot easily adjust to precise mass capabilities, which require different kinds of training and entirely new conceptions of how to fight. Exquisite systems, for instance, are scarce, so units must take great care not to waste systems and to minimize the risk of destruction. With precise mass, by contrast, units are supposed to move quickly and not make the perfect the enemy of the good. This helps explain why the United States has struggled to adapt to precise mass—even though the country invented precision guidance and boasts the best military in the world.
Iran, meanwhile, has been broadly locked out of some more advanced military capabilities. As a result, it had to invest heavily in long-range, one-way attack systems and cheap ballistic missiles. The result is a war in which Iran has dramatically outperformed expectations. Tehran could not go blow for blow with the U.S. military’s exquisite weapons, but it did not need to, because it could rapidly fire relatively accurate drones and cheap missiles at U.S. bases and the region’s critical infrastructure. The United States has dealt billions of dollars of damage to Iran in turn, but only by burning through its stockpiles of Tomahawks, SM-6 missiles, and other expensive systems. As a result, Washington now has to sprint to resupply its own stocks and those of partners elsewhere, such as Taiwan and Ukraine.
 Weaker states are no longer priced out of the military power game.
Thanks to rigorous preparations, meanwhile, Tehran has been able to withstand the extensive damage. In the years before the war, Iran built a vast underground network of missile infrastructure spread across its territory that has proved impossible for U.S. and Israeli forces to eliminate thus far. The United States had even more trouble destroying Iran’s heavily dispersed missile production facilities, inverting assumptions that have guided American airpower campaigns since Operation Desert Storm against Iraq in 1991, where the emphasis was destroying existing weapons stockpiles.
Iran has shown that weaker states are no longer priced out of the military power game, and the United States has discovered that stronger states are not guaranteed the upper hand in major battles. Little wonder, then, that countries rich and poor are investing in precise mass. North Korea, for example, has received Iran’s Shahed technology and production equipment from Russia and is using it to develop its own cheap uncrewed vehicles. A company in Nigeria has contracted with a Turkish manufacturer to build 100,000 one-way attack drones at local assembly facilities. Poland has increased spending on drones and counterdrone systems from about $27 million in late 2023 to roughly $6.9 billion this year and established domestic drone factories. Six European states, including France, Germany, and the United Kingdom, signed a letter of intent to jointly develop a one-way attack drone with a range of over 300 miles and a target cost of less than $100,000. Saudi Arabia has unveiled its own attack drone modeled on the Shahed with a supposed range of more than 900 miles. And Japan’s governing party has requested a record $55.6 billion defense budget, largely so that it can buy great quantities of attack drones.
OFFENSE OVER DEFENSE
The Iran war shows that nearly every military can acquire lots of precision strike weapons that cost tens of thousands of dollars apiece. But defense remains much more expensive. There are very few reliable interceptors that cost less than $1 million. To repel Iran’s precise mass, Washington had to use about 65 percent of its Patriot interceptors and 35 percent of its THAAD interceptors, leaving it with roughly 1,000 and 250 of each type, respectively. The country’s partners in the Middle East are also running out of air defenses.
For the United States, this challenge was inevitable. The exclusive focus on exquisite systems since the end of the Cold War extended to how it approached defense, emphasizing antimissile systems intended to stop high-end ballistic and cruise missile attacks. Meanwhile, policymakers assumed that wars would be short, so they did not focus on designing defenses that could be easily scaled.
Now, Washington and other governments are trying to come up with cheaper defensive systems, experimenting with technologies such as directed energy weapons and high-power microwave systems that could destroy incoming drones. They are looking at interceptor systems that simply need to get near drones and explode to destroy them, rather than actually make contact head on. The international market has started to move: Ukraine is fielding interceptor drones that cost just $1,400 apiece, and European and Gulf-based startups are likewise building cheaper interceptors. But none of these systems appears ready to scale now.
The Iran war has also highlighted American capabilities that should prove useful in the new era of warfare. Over the last few years, AI that aggregates intelligence from many sources and cues up targeting recommendations for commanders has become an essential part of conflict, giving the United States—with its many AI companies and experience building so-called decision-support platforms—an advantage. Washington, for example, fielded the Maven Smart System, allowing it to dramatically increase the rate of its military strikes. This system has not been flawless; it may, for example, have mistakenly flagged an Iranian school as a target after relying on faulty intelligence inputs it was not enabled to check, contributing to a strike that killed over 100 children. The incredible speed of targeting selection also increases the risk of automation bias, whereby humans will outsource cognition to imperfect algorithms, leading to errors. But the system has apparently made targeting relatively more accurate, and the U.S. military can implement reforms that would make targeting mistakes even less likely. That means the binding constraint on how quickly a U.S. campaign could move is no longer intelligence processing, but inventory.
