articles.title: Time To Fund the OPCW - Center for Arms Control and Non-Proliferation
articles.summary: Time To Fund the OPCW  Center for Arms Control and Non-Proliferation

source_detail.name: Center for Arms Control and Non-Proliferation

articles.full_text:
By John Erath
Since 1993, chemical weapons have killed thousands, with many times more affected, often suffering for years. This despite the Chemical Weapons Convention ban on such activity and a general view that such weapons have little military utility and too high a risk of harm to civilians. During that time, the Organization for the Prevention of Chemical Weapons, the OPCW, has led international efforts to halt chemical weapons use. The OPCW has done valuable work, including in Syria and Ukraine to identify users of chemical weapons and put a stop to their production before use. The good work is now in jeopardy because the United States has not paid its contribution.
Funding the OPCW is clearly in the U.S. interest as it has time and again kept chemical weapons from falling into the hands of terrorists who would have little hesitation about using such weapons against Americans. OPCW has traditionally enjoyed strong bipartisan support in Washington, so this is not about politics. Rather, the OPCW appears to have been caught in general skepticism about international organizations. It deserves better.
Greg Koblenz, a member of the Center’s Scientists Working Group on Biological and Chemical Security has written a letter, co-signed by 18 leading experts on chemical weapons and non-proliferation from across the political spectrum, on the importance of funding the OPCW. The letter is addressed to Secretary of State Rubio and reads as follows:
Dear Mr. Secretary and National Security Advisor Rubio,
International efforts to reduce the threat posed by chemical weapons are being endangered by the failure of the United States to pay its annual contribution to the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW), the international organization charged with implementing the 1993 Chemical Weapons Convention that bans the production and use of chemical weapons. Full and effective implementation of the Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC) is vital to U.S. national security.
The CWC has historically enjoyed strong bipartisan support in the United States. The treaty was drafted during the Ronald Reagan and George H.W. Bush administrations and ratified by the Republican-controlled Senate in 1997. The OPCW won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2013 for its intensive efforts to eliminate chemical weapons.
The United States, the largest contributor to the OPCW, has not paid the $17 million it owes for 2026. To put that amount into perspective, the overdue payment is one-fifth of the OPCW’s annual budget of $90 million, which the United States voted in favor of last year.
As a result of the lack of timely payment by the United States, the OPCW’s independent financial advisory board has warned that the organization is in a “precarious” financial situation and faces the “unprecedented circumstance” of having to cancel or postpone routine activities like inspections and verification missions. These are strong words from otherwise mild-mannered accountants. In July, the accountants predicted that these cancellations and postponements could start as early as mid-August so the OPCW may have already started curtailing its operations due to this funding crunch.
This is no time to shortchange the OPCW. We, the undersigned nonproliferation and national security experts, urge the United States to pay its assessed contribution as soon as possible to avoid any disruption to the OPCW’s activities, which are vital to our own security.
The global chemical weapon landscape remains complex and challenging. The OPCW is currently engaged in operations in Syria and Ukraine and new missions involving Sudan and Cambodia/Thailand are on the horizon.
In Syria, the OPCW is finally making progress locating, securing, and destroying the remnants of the Assad regime’s chemical weapons program. In May, OPCW experts confirmed the discovery of dozens of Assad-era chemical weapons and in August they began supervising Syria’s destruction of these weapons. So far, just over half of these weapons have been destroyed while Syrian teams and OPCW inspectors search the country for more. The OPCW has also undertaken training missions to build the capacity of the Syrian government to find, secure, and destroy chemical weapons left over from the Assad regime.
Russia continues using chemicals as weapons against Ukraine at an unprecedented scale with almost 14,000 reported incidents since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. The United States and multiple European governments have accused Russia of using riot control agents and chloropicrin, a World War I-era vomiting agent, on the battlefield in Ukraine. The OPCW has deployed teams five times to Ukraine to investigate Russia’s use of chemical weapons and confirmed Ukrainian allegations that riot control agents have been used on the battlefield. The OPCW has also trained Ukrainian experts in the detection of chemical warfare agents, how to safely collect and transport chemical samples, and how to respond to the use of toxic chemicals.
Recent reports of chemical weapon use by Sudan and Thailand could place new demands on the OPCW that are not covered by its regular budget.
Since the United States first accused Sudan in May 2025 of using chemical weapons against the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) as part of that country’s civil war, credible evidence has recently emerged that strongly supports this allegation. According to these sources, Sudan used chlorine-filled cylinders in at least two attacks in September 2024 and produced a stockpile of aerial bombs designed to disperse chlorine gas. Earlier this month, Cambodia filed a complaint with the OPCW alleging that Thailand had used unspecified chemical weapons during a 2025 border skirmish.
The allegations regarding Sudan and Thailand could potentially trigger an investigation of alleged use, a technical assistance visit, or, in the case of Sudan, a challenge inspection of suspected chemical weapon facilities. Any of these deployments would place new demands on the OPCW’s inspectors and laboratory.
We urge you to direct that the administration deliver the United States full assessed contribution for the OPCW’s vital work by the start of the next Executive Council session on October 6.
Respectfully,
Philipp C. Bleek, Professor, Middlebury Institute of International Studies at Monterey
Stefano Costanzi, Professor of Chemistry and Policy, American University
Nancy D. Connell, Professor Emerita, Rutgers New Jersey Medical School
John Erath, Senior Policy Director, Center for Arms Control and Non-Proliferation
Anemone Franz, Visiting Research Fellow, American Enterprise Institute
Col. (ret) John A. Gilbert, Senior Science Fellow, Scientists Working Group on Chemical and Biological Security, Center for Arms Control and Non-Proliferation; former Chief of the Chemical Inspection Division, On-Site Inspection Agency (now Defense Threat Reduction Agency), Department of Defense
Natasha H. Hall, former Community Engagement Director, Mayday Rescue
Dan Kaszeta, Fellow of the Royal Historical Society
Daryl G. Kimball, Executive Director, Arms Control Association
Jeffrey W. Knopf, Professor, Monterey Institute of International Studies
Gregory D. Koblentz, Associate Professor & Director, Biodefense Graduate Program, George Mason University
Margaret E. Kosal, Professor, Sam Nunn School of International Affairs, Georgia Institute of Technology
Albert J. Mauroni, former director, US Air Force Center for Strategic Deterrence Studies
Christina McAllister, Partnerships in Proliferation Prevention Program Director, Henry L. Stimson Center
Amb. (ret) Robert Mikulak, former U.S. Permanent Representative to the OPCW
Saskia Popescu, Adjunct Faculty, Biodefense Graduate Program, George Mason University
Mallory Stewart, Chief Executive Officer, Council on Strategic Risks
Andrea Stricker, Deputy Director, Nonproliferation Program, Foundation for Defense of Democracies
Paul F. Walker, Chair, Chemical Weapons Convention Coalition; Vice Chair, Arms Control Association
*Affiliations are for identification purposes only. The views expressed are those of the signatories in their personal capacity and do not necessarily represent the views or positions of their respective institutions.
CC: Senator Dave McCormick, SFRC; Senator Rand Paul, SFRC; Senator Tammy Duckworth, SFRC; Senator Chris Coons, SFRC; Senator Tim Kaine, SFRC; Congressman Ryan Mackenzie, HFAC; Congressman Michael Baumgartner; Congressman Mike McCaul, HFAC; Congressman Greg Meeks, HFAC; Congresswoman Sara Jacobs, HFAC; Congressman Gabe Amo, HFRC; Congresswoman Sarah McBride; and Congressman Mark Pocan
As the letter states, it is time to act and release the funding for the OPCW. State’s own FY26 and FY27 budget justifications cite OPCW as important for U.S. national security. This has not changed.
This is not a political matter. It is a case of U.S. interest. Let’s hope the administration does the right thing.

articles.title: Inside the UK’s new security centre fighting deepfakes and information warfare - ADS Advance
articles.summary: Inside the UK’s new security centre fighting deepfakes and information warfare  ADS Advance
articles.full_text:
The UK is creating a new national security centre to identify and disrupt hostile information campaigns as artificial intelligence makes it easier for foreign states to spread convincing disinformation and deepfakes.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced the National Centre for Information Defence during his first address to the United Nations General Assembly in New York.
The centre will bring together government departments, intelligence agencies, law enforcement and technology companies to counter information operations directed against the UK.
Burnham said hostile states were mounting what he described as an “industrial-scale assault” on the UK and its allies. He singled out Russia, accusing its agencies of using bots, fake websites and falsified news articles to influence public opinion.
“Russian agencies have used every means at their disposal to spread lies and disinformation and prey on people’s fear,” Burnham told the UN.
The announcement puts information warfare more firmly alongside cyberattacks, espionage and sabotage as a national security threat.
What is the National Centre for Information Defence?
The new centre will detect, attribute and disrupt information attacks by foreign states.
The UK’s existing National Cyber Security Centre is the country’s technical authority for cyber security and helps protect government, businesses and critical infrastructure from cyberattacks.
The National Centre for Information Defence will instead focus on attempts to manipulate the information environment. These could include networks of fake social-media accounts, fabricated websites, forged material presented as coming from legitimate organisations and AI-generated images, audio and video.
The centre will initially be led from the Office for the Prime Minister and Cabinet, working with intelligence agencies, government departments, police and social-media companies.
How the UK monitors disinformation
The UK is not starting from scratch on fighting disinformation. The government already operates the National Security Online Information Team (NSOIT), which identifies and responds to misinformation and deliberate disinformation that pose risks to national security or public safety.
The government describes NSOIT’s work as analysing publicly available information, including social-media activity, to identify attempts to manipulate the online information environment.
The Defending Democracy Taskforce also coordinates work across government, Parliament, intelligence agencies and police to protect the UK’s democratic system from foreign interference.
The new centre would provide a more centralised capability focused specifically on hostile information operations. The government has not yet published full details of its staffing, budget or how its responsibilities will overlap with existing bodies.
AI intensifies the threat
In his UN speech, Burnham linked the decision directly to advances in artificial intelligence.
Generative AI can produce convincing text, images, cloned voices and video quickly and at scale. Deepfakes can make fabricated statements or events appear authentic, potentially making information operations more difficult to identify.
Burnham said the Kremlin spends around £1.3 billion annually manipulating information.
“We’re talking about an insidious campaign that reaches into people’s homes and twists what they feel about their own country and community – creating a narrative of decline, stoking division and sowing despair,” he said.
The UK’s National Security Strategy identifies technology-enabled hybrid threats as a growing security challenge.
From detecting propaganda to disrupting it
The centre’s stated mission to detect, attribute and disrupt hostile information operations suggests the UK wants to go beyond monitoring and rebutting false information. It is not yet clear exactly what “disrupt” would involve.
Responses could include exposing coordinated foreign campaigns, sharing intelligence with allies and working with online platforms over accounts or material that breach their rules.
Existing NSOIT policy offers some indication of the boundaries. It analyses publicly available material rather than private communications. When it identifies content that may breach a social-media company’s policies, it can alert the platform, but the platform decides whether to remove it.
Whether the new centre will have broader powers remains unclear.
Protecting elections from foreign interference
Elections are likely to be among the centre’s most sensitive responsibilities.
Burnham told the UN that Britain has evidence Russia attempted to interfere in the 2019 general election.
“They’ve used bots and fake websites. Falsified newspaper articles. Forged the branding of 28 British organisations – including universities and the BBC,” he said. “They’ve amplified far-right narratives.”
Russia has denied allegations that it interferes in other countries’ democratic processes.
The government has already strengthened coordination between political parties, the Electoral Commission and security services over foreign interference. Its response to the Rycroft Review also called for online information threats to be more closely integrated into the UK’s wider national-security framework.
A new front in UK national security: building trust through information security
The National Centre for Information Defence reflects an evolution of how the UK approaches national security.
Protecting the country increasingly goes beyond defending borders, infrastructure and computer networks to identifying attempts by hostile states to manipulate the information people see and trust.
Existing government structures distinguish between inaccurate or misleading information and disinformation deliberately created to cause harm. NSOIT’s work is limited to threats affecting public safety or national security. The remit and safeguards governing the new centre have yet to be announced.
For now, it is clear that the UK intends to treat coordinated foreign information operations as security threats that can be detected, attributed and disrupted to build trust rather than merely rebutted after they spread and do harm.

articles.title: India’s UN Security Council Bid gets ‘Historic’ Backing: Why is it seeking a permanent seat for 30 years? Is it possible now? - Jagran Josh
articles.summary: India’s UN Security Council Bid gets ‘Historic’ Backing: Why is it seeking a permanent seat for 30 years? Is it possible now?  Jagran Josh
articles.full_text:
The UNSC presently has 15 members: five permanent members — the United States, Russia, China, France and the United Kingdom — and 10 non-permanent members elected for two-year terms. The permanent five or the P5, have veto power over several resolutions.
India’s bid for a permanent seat on the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) has received diplomatic backing, with Hungary, Poland, Slovakia and the Czech Republic supporting India’s candidature at the Visegrad Group (V4)-India foreign ministers’ meeting on September 22 in New York. The development comes as India sustaining its campaign for Security Council reform and a higher role for the Global South.
The group agreed to deepen cooperation in political, economic, technological, and defence and people-to-people ties, on the margins of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly.
“It was, in a sense, a new historic occasion,” Jaishankar said after the meeting.
What is India seeking?
The UNSC presently has 15 members: five permanent members — the United States, Russia, China, France and the United Kingdom — and 10 non-permanent members elected for two-year terms. The permanent five or the P5, have veto power over several resolutions.
India has served eight times as a non-permanent member, most recently in 2021-22. Now, India is seeking permanent membership, arguing that the Council’s structure, established in 1945, does not proportionately represent current geopolitical issues or developing countries’ representation.
Why does India want a permanent seat?
A permanent seat would offer India continuous representation on the Council rather than needing periodic elections. It would also facilitate a long-term role in decisions concerning international peace and security, including sanctions, conflicts and global security issues.
India has linked its demand to broader reform of the UN system and more representation for Asia, Africa and Latin America. It is also part of the G4 grouping with Brazil, Germany and Japan, which is also demanding for extension of the Council in both permanent and non-permanent categories. Turkiye, too has urged for the abolition of veto power.
Related Stories
Which countries support India’s UNSC seat efforts?
France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States have backed India’s permanent membership in various official statements. The freshsupport from the four V4 countries adds to India’s diplomatic push.
However, support for India’s candidature does not naturally mean agreement on the structure of an expanded Council. Unresolved contested concerns pile up over the number of new seats, regional representation, veto rights and the claims of other countries.
What is China’s stance?
China remains crucial because it is one of the five existing permanent members and has a decisive role in any UN Charter amendment. Previously, China has supported India and Brazil playing a greater role in the United Nations, including the Security Council, but has not replicated the same agreement openly for India’s permanent seat bid as France, Russia, the UK and US.
Russia Backs India’s UNSC Permanent Seat Bid
Addressing world leaders at the 81st United Nations General Assembly, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said any reform of the UN Security Council must preserve the Council’s existing powers, including those of its permanent members. Moscow also opposed any reform that would result in additional permanent seats being given to Western countries.
Lavrov called for a more inclusive and geographically balanced global architecture, while strongly supporting greater representation for countries from the Global South. He said Russia favoured expanding the representation of Asia, Africa and Latin America in the Security Council.
“We are in favour of broadening the representation of Asia, Africa, and Latin America. We support Brazil's and India's candidatures for a permanent seat,” Lavrov said.
He also stressed the need to address the interests of the African continent as part of any future reform process.
Russia’s support adds to growing backing for India’s long-standing campaign for permanent membership of the UN Security Council. Several countries voiced support for New Delhi’s candidature during the 81st UNGA session, while also calling for reforms to make the Council more representative of contemporary geopolitical and economic realities.
Mauritius was among the countries supporting India’s bid. Foreign Minister Dhananjay Ramful said Mauritius supported the positions of the G4 and L69 groups on Security Council reform and reiterated its backing for India’s candidature for a permanent seat, citing the country’s constructive role in global affairs.
India has also received support through the G4 grouping, which includes India, Brazil, Germany and Japan. Marshall Islands President Hilda Heine reaffirmed her country’s support for the G4 and said the Marshall Islands backed Japan and its G4 partners in their efforts to secure permanent membership of the Security Council.
Why are challenges to India’s UNSC permanent seat bid?
India cannot simply be voted into a vacant permanent seat because no such seat exists under the present UN Charter. Establish more permanent seats necessitates Charter reform.
Under Article 108, an amendment must be adopted by a two-thirds majority of the UN General Assembly and ratified by two-thirds of UN members, including all five permanent UNSC members.
The future of Security Council
India is prepping for a ninth elected term on the Security Council for 2028-29, with elections slated for June 2027. Its permanent-seat campaign dwells on broader and inclusive negotiations over the Council’s future structure and long-term reforms.
At Jagran Josh, she specialises in writing explainers and analytical stories on international news and current affairs. Over the years, she has developed strong expertise in leveraging digital and multimedia tools, along with SEO best practices, to enhance the speed, reach, and impact of her stories.

articles.title: Moscow says: We would not want Tehran to withdraw from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty - fakti.bg
articles.summary: Moscow says: We would not want Tehran to withdraw from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty  fakti.bg
articles.full_text:
Russia would not want Iran to withdraw from the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT) and relies on the Islamic Republic to continue participating in the agreement, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said today, quoted by Reuters, BTA reports.
Peskov said this in response to comments by Iranian officials regarding Tehran's possible withdrawal from the treaty, which commits the Islamic Republic not to develop or acquire nuclear weapons.
Russia and Iran maintain close ties under a strategic cooperation agreement between the two countries, Reuters recalls.
Peskov also said that placing foreign companies' assets in Russia under temporary management does not constitute a change in their ownership and is partly a response to the increasing involvement of “hostile countries“ in military actions against Russia.
Russian authorities this month transferred control of assets in Russia of Swiss food giant “Nestle“, German retail group “Metro“ and French retail group “Auchan“.
Peskov said the measures were reversible, but Moscow currently saw no reason to lift them.
“Given the increasing level of involvement of these hostile countries in direct military actions against our country, such decisions are being made,“ he said.

Iran will consider the proposal to withdraw from the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT), deputy speaker of parliament Ali Nikzad said.
“The draft to withdraw from the NPT is being discussed with extreme urgency. As soon as it is submitted to parliament, it will be discussed on the same day,” Nikzad said, Fars news agency reports.

articles.title: ICC took no steps to withdraw Netanyahu arrest warrant, deputy prosecutor says - Middle East Eye
articles.summary: ICC took no steps to withdraw Netanyahu arrest warrant, deputy prosecutor says  Middle East Eye
articles.full_text:
The International Criminal Court (ICC) has taken no steps to withdraw arrest warrants or related applications concerning Israeli officials, despite mounting pressure and sanctions from the United States, Deputy Prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan has said.
“The case is still proceeding,” Khan told CNN in a weekend interview.
“We have taken no steps to try and withdraw any of those arrest warrant applications or the arrest warrants themselves, and the team continues to investigate in that situation.”
The ICC issued arrest warrants in November 2024 for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his then defence minister, Yoav Gallant, over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in Gaza since October 2023.
Since then, the US has imposed sanctions on most of the court's leadership, including the former chief prosecutor Karim Khan, the two deputy prosecutors, and nine judges including the court's president.
Israel has also taken steps to challenge the warrants at the ICC. Two appeals remain in progress, including one challenging the court's jurisdiction over Israeli nationals because Israel is not a member of the court.
Meanwhile, Middle East Eye has reported that the prosecutor’s office had pursued further cases against senior Israeli officials over the past two years.
In May, MEE reported that the prosecutor’s office had filed a confidential application seeking arrest for Israel’s Finance Minister Bezalal Smotrich over alleged crimes committed against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.
The charges included forced displacement as both a war crime and crime against humanity, transferring Israel’s civilian population into occupied territory as a war crime, and persecution and apartheid as crimes against humanity.
An evidence review had also been held to consider two further applications, including one targeting National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir.
'We have trials in court'
Khan’s comments came amid an escalating campaign by the administration of US President Donald Trump against the Hague-based court.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced in July that Washington would use every tool at its disposal to “dismantle the ICC – brick by brick, if necessary”, while urging member states to withdraw their support for the institution.
In other press statements, Rubio also described the court as a “stupid organisation” run by “lunatics and crazies”, and warned that it would face consequences for attempting to exercise jurisdiction over American nationals.
Khan said the court remained grounded in the Rome Statute, its founding treaty, which was adopted through the sovereign decisions of its member states after decades of negotiations.
“The work of the court continues unabated,” she said.
“We have trials in court. We have a trial scheduled for November of this year and one for next year. We have, in the course of the last year, seen convictions in two major trials, and we continue to conduct our investigations and our prosecutions, and appear in court on a regular basis, regardless of these events.”
Established in 2002, the ICC is the only permanent international court with the jurisdiction to prosecute senior officials for war crimes, crimes against humanity, genocide and the crime of aggression.
In addition to the Palestine investigation, the court has more than a dozen active situations, including Ukraine, Darfur, Libya and Afghanistan.
Khan acknowledged that the court and its staff were operating under considerable pressure.
“The nature of the work that we do means that we inevitably will face pressure of all sorts to try and toe a political line, for instance, or to take a different position on the charging of accused persons, or to follow a path in investigation and prosecution,” she said.
“So, indeed, we do feel pressure, but, as I’ve said, the dedication of our staff is extraordinary, and they continue to do their work.”
Washington sanctioned Khan and fellow Deputy Prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang in August 2025, alongside two ICC judges. The sanctions froze any US-based assets they held and prohibited American individuals and companies from providing them with funds, goods or services.
Describing the personal consequences, Khan said sanctioned officials could lose access to banks and have their credit cards revoked, while financial transactions in Europe could be restricted to the Single Euro Payments Area.
'We do feel pressure, but, as I’ve said, the dedication of our staff is extraordinary, and they continue to do their work'
- Nazhat Khan, ICC deputy prosecutor
Other service providers, including health insurance companies, might also sever ties, she said, while family members could be prevented from entering the US.
“I was never given any reasons for the sanctioning,” Khan said. “However, I believe it was because I am a deputy prosecutor at the Office of the Prosecutor.”
The Trump administration is now reportedly preparing broader sanctions against the ICC as an institution, potentially cutting it off from dollar transactions and hitting its access to banking, insurance and technology services.
Despite the pressure, Khan said she remained hopeful about the future of international law.
“The work that we do for victims, the fact that we continue to hear their voices stridently, with so much sincerity – they believe in this court,” she said.
“For them, this provides an avenue of justice that may not necessarily be provided in many courts around the world.
“Every single member of this court works for humanity,” she added, “and there can be nothing better than that.”

articles.title: Czech PM Andrej Babis reiterates importance of NATO but rejects calls to increase defense spending - dw.com
articles.summary: Czech PM Andrej Babis reiterates importance of NATO but rejects calls to increase defense spending  dw.com
articles.full_text:
The Czech Republic "must remain committed to increasing defense spending," Matthew Whitaker, the US envoy to NATO, demanded in Prague last week. "We expect our allies to step up," he said.
The call is nothing new. As warnings about the threat emanating from Russia increase, and Washington demands European allies take greater responsibility for security, NATO has raised its target for defense spending from 2% to 3.5% of GDP, and pressure on those lagging is rising.
Czechia, alongside Slovenia and Albania, has yet to meet the old target. But Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis, whose government cut the defense budget for 2026 to around 1.7% of GDP when it took office late last year, pushed back against the latest barb from Washington.
While reiterating that NATO membership is crucial for Czechia, the premier bluntly stated that the government cannot afford to accelerate spending. He has pledged to hit the 2% target in 2027 but plans no further increases.
That leaves the populist billionaire hoping that a personal rapport with US President Donald Trump will protect the country amid the burgeoning row.
Warnings of a growing threat
Whether Trump will protect Czechia from the threat of Russian hybrid warfare targeting Central European NATO allies is another question.
A growing wave of stray drones and Russian intelligence operations — suspected bombings, sabotage and cyber warfare — have spread alarm in the neighborhood.
Germany and Poland — key Czech partners — have reported high-profile incidents and linked them to attempts to intimidate Ukrainian allies.
Czechia should understand the threat better than most, having been among the first to experience such an attack.
Czechia's Security Information Service (BIS) reported in 2021 that the bombing of a depot storing weapons linked to Ukraine seven years previously had been carried out by Russia's domestic intelligence agency, the Federal Security Service (FSB).
Babis, then in his first stint as PM, responded by expelling around 100 Russian diplomats and embassy staff, freezing relations with Moscow.
The BIS remains in step with other intelligence agencies across the region in warning that the threat from Russia is growing.
However, like its predecessors, the Babis government has failed to keep pace in terms of the national defense budget, even as neighbors have leapt into action.
Prague spent just 1.86% of GDP on defense last year; Poland and the Baltic States have already met the new NATO target and will hit 5% next year.
Prague's priorities
Babis has made it clear this approach will not change. However, his claim that Czechia can't afford to boost defense spending is at odds with the 2027 budget his government approved on September 22.
The fiscal plan will expand expenditure generously and targets Czechia's second-highest deficit ever at 386 billion Czech crowns (€15.8 billion or $18 billion).
While finally catching up to the old NATO target will account for some of that spending, most of the increased outlay will reflect the coalition government's domestic political priorities.
The plan clearly reflects the election campaign promises of Babis's ANO party and its junior partners, the far-right Freedom and Direct Democracy party (SPD) and radical-right Motorists for Themselves party. They all say defense can't be allowed to disrupt the urgent need to spend on pensions, education, healthcare and infrastructure.
"The claim that the country cannot spend more on defense is primarily rooted in domestic politics," Ales Michal, a political scientist at Prague's Charles University, told DW. "The major priority is investment in the social system."
That will be welcomed by supporters of the governing parties, who skew older and less well off, and resent the support being given to 300,000 or so Ukrainian refugees.
"None of the governing parties promised voters higher defense spending," in campaigning for last year's election, Michal notes.
Critics, however, say that's because the government is downplaying the threat from Russia. The government's spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment.
'We don't want World War III'
The reticence to raise defense spending also reflects political narratives around the war in Ukraine.
Two days after Whitaker's rebuke, Babis appeared in a video dressed in a T-shirt emblazoned with the words "No War" in blue and yellow letters. While he noted the threat from Russia, he called for greater efforts to find peace.
"We don't want World War III, do we?" he pronounced, repeating his claim that Europe should work harder to end the conflict.
It was a performance echoing the stance of Europe's radical right-wing, and the sort that has seen the Czech PM labelled "pro-Russian" in some international media.
The truth is more mundane. Babis is a pragmatist. The ANO electorate is populist and anti-Ukrainian, but also strongly pro-Western. Surveys show that the plan to keep defense spending at 2% of GDP precisely matches its views.
Yet Babis's divisive personality leaves the party dependent on extremist partners for enough support to govern, and so he must also try to speak the anti-system, pro-Russian language of the SPD, which, despite controlling the defense ministry, was pushing to cut spending further in the 2027 budget.
"A critical stance towards Ukraine also shapes the government's position on spending," said Michal. The pro-peace stance downplaying Russia's aggression moves ANO "closer to the European radical right," he notes, but Babis is "guided by opinion polls," and must try to find a "balance between two polarizing positions."
Strategic understanding
The opposition sees this dichotomy as the government's Achilles' heel.
Martin Kupka, leader of the center-right Civic Democrats (ODS), welcomed Babis's reiterated NATO commitment before asking the PM: "When will you get rid of the Kremlin fifth column, which you took into the government and even entrusted with the Ministry of Defense?"
However, although the ODS-led government that held office between 2021 and 2025 offered fervent support to Ukraine, like all its predecessors, it also failed to meet the NATO spending target.
"Our partners may be unhappy about the approach to spending, but it's the reality of the political situation in our country," Andor Sandor, a defense analyst and former commander of Czechia's Military Intelligence Service, told DW.
However, he added that while weak defense spending growth "is not optimal," the biggest issue is a lack of strategic understanding regarding the military's size and role.
Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan
